blocks.text: Jonathan Zecher’s 2025 historical study places Dorotheus in sixth-century Gaza and describes education in rhetoric, philosophy, and medicine. Its introduction identifies service under Seridus and guidance from Barsanuphius and John. The article notes the guesthouse and infirmary responsibilities and distinguishes Dorotheus’s later monastery from the community in which he trained.

blocks.text: The study treats the surviving Instructions, Letters, and Sayings as material from his abbacy. Its section The Last of the Gazans situates them in oral teaching to monks and the late-antique educational setting. The article’s disputed reconstruction of Origenist influence is an academic thesis; this biography does not recast that thesis as the Church’s teaching or use it to merge Dorotheus with the Egyptian namesake.

blocks.text:
And there came thither certain Jews from Antioch and Iconium, who persuaded the people, and, having stoned Paul, drew him out of the city, supposing he had been dead.

Howbeit, as the disciples stood round about him, he rose up, and came into the city: and the next day he departed with Barnabas to Derbe.

And when they had preached the gospel to that city, and had taught many, they returned again to Lystra, and to Iconium, and Antioch,

Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.

And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
blocks.context: Acts14: 22 is specifically cited in the OCA account of Dorotheus’s concern about tribulations. The quotation supplies the biblical context, not an episode in Dorotheus’s own life.

blocks.text: The OCA traces a reception beyond his own monastery: Russian manuscript collections circulated his Instructions with the replies of Barsanuphius and John, and with The Ladder and Ephraim’s works. It specifically names Cyril of White Lake as a later abbot who copied Dorotheus’s Discourses by hand. This is the source’s account of transmission, not a new reading rule assigned here.
